message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
I believe this is one of the strongest applications we have put together. The need is documented, not asserted: our household numbers are up by around two-thirds in two years, and we can quantify exactly how much fresh food we are turning away, 1.2 tonnes a week, because we log every declined offer. The project responds directly to that gap and nothing more. The budget is lean: we got competing quotes for the cold room and the electrics and took the lower figure each time, and the van comes with a warranty. The value for money is exceptional, at roughly 33p per meal in the first year and falling to almost nothing over the equipment's ten-year life. We have thought about the long term too: this is a one-off capital investment with written supermarket commitments behind it, so it will keep delivering without coming back to funders. Our monitoring is concrete and measurable. I am confident the Foundation will see this as exactly the kind of lasting capacity-building its fund exists for.
</author>

Your review is being evaluated on whether it identifies the problems in the document.

<document>
Grant Application: Chilled Storage for Fresh Food Distribution
Applicant: Hollins Valley Food Bank (registered charity)
To: Ashworth Community Foundation, Community Resilience Fund (capital grants)
Amount requested: £48,600

1. About us
Hollins Valley Food Bank has provided emergency food to households in the valley since 2014. We are run by two part-time paid staff and around 70 volunteers, and we operate from a warehouse in Hollinsford and three distribution sites in Hollinsford, Brackley Bridge and Over Hollins, which open on different days of the week. Referrals come from GPs, schools, Citizens Advice and the local authority's welfare team.

2. The need
Demand has risen sharply. The number of households we supported rose from an average of 410 a week in 2023 to 620 a week in 2025, an increase of 66%. Over the same period our food donations have changed in character. Supermarket surplus schemes now offer us large volumes of fresh produce, dairy and chilled ready meals, but we have no chilled storage beyond three domestic fridges, so we currently decline around 1.2 tonnes of fresh food each week. Our parcels are therefore dominated by tinned and dried goods, and clients, referrers and our own volunteers consistently tell us that families want fresh food, particularly for children.

3. The project
We are seeking funding to:
- install a 12 cubic metre walk-in cold room at our Hollinsford warehouse;
- buy a used refrigerated van, so that chilled food can be collected from supermarket depots and taken to our four distribution sites at safe temperatures;
- upgrade the warehouse electrical supply to support the cold room.

With these in place we could accept the 1.2 tonnes a week we currently decline, about 62 tonnes a year. Using the national food-redistribution conversion of 2,380 meals per tonne, that is around 147,600 additional meals a year, at a one-off capital cost of about 33p per meal in the first year alone.

4. Budget
Item | Cost
Walk-in cold room, supply and installation | £26,400
Refrigerated van (three years old, 40,000 miles) | £18,500
Electrical supply upgrade | £3,700
Total requested | £48,600

Quotes from two suppliers were obtained for the cold room and the electrical work; the lower quote is shown in each case. The van price is from a commercial dealer and includes a 12-month warranty.

5. Running costs
We have obtained estimates for the additional running costs. The cold room will add around £4,200 a year to our electricity bill. Insurance, fuel, servicing and road tax for the van will cost around £6,800 a year. Our 2025 accounts show total income of £96,000, almost all of it restricted to food purchasing and staff costs, an unrestricted surplus of £900, and unrestricted reserves of £5,100.

6. Outcomes and monitoring
We will measure:
- tonnes of fresh and chilled food received and distributed each month;
- the proportion of parcels containing fresh produce (currently under 10%; target 80% within six months);
- client feedback through our quarterly survey.
We will report to the Foundation at six and twelve months.

7. Timetable
The cold room supplier can install within eight weeks of order. We would order on award, with the cold room and van in service by October 2026.

8. Sustainability
This is a one-off capital investment. Once installed, the cold room and van will be sustainable without further grant funding, and will serve the valley for at least ten years. Our partner supermarkets have confirmed in writing that they will continue to offer us surplus fresh food.

9. Why fund us
The Foundation's Community Resilience Fund aims to strengthen local organisations' long-term capacity to meet need. This project does exactly that: a modest capital investment that permanently transforms the quality of the food we can give to families, at a very low cost per meal.
</document>
response:
# Review: Hollins Valley Food Bank Chilled Storage Application

The case for fresh food is well framed and the budget is clearly laid out. But a funder reading closely will find one problem that undermines the application, and several errors that will cost credibility. These should be fixed before submission.

## 1. Critical: the running costs can't be met, so the sustainability claim fails

Section 5 says the project adds about **£11,000 a year** in running costs: £4,200 for electricity and £6,800 for the van. The same section shows:
- an unrestricted surplus of **£900**;
- unrestricted reserves of **£5,100**;
- income that is "almost all restricted to food purchasing and staff costs."

The application never says who pays the £11,000. On these figures, reserves would cover about five or six months, after which the van and cold room could not run. Section 8 then states the project "will be sustainable without further grant funding." Section 5 directly contradicts this. A capital assessor will notice, because this is exactly the risk capital funds look for: equipment bought and then left idle.

To fix it, add a funded running-cost plan, such as:
- committed revenue funding;
- a supermarket or corporate contribution to fuel and electricity;
- a fundraising target with evidence it is realistic;
- savings elsewhere (for example, less spending on tinned and dried food if fresh surplus replaces it).

Without this, Sections 8 and 9 and the "won't come back to funders" message should not go in as written.

The running-cost estimate is also probably incomplete:
- The van comes with only a **12-month warranty**. After that, repairs on a vehicle that is three years old at purchase are unbudgeted.
- There is no cost for cold-room maintenance or a refrigeration service contract.
- There is no money set aside to replace the van, which will not last the claimed ten years (see 4).

## 2. Arithmetic error in the headline need figure

410 to 620 households a week is a **51%** increase, not 66% (210 ÷ 410 = 0.512). "Around two-thirds" is also wrong. The real increase is still strong. An error in the very first statistic invites the reader to doubt every other figure, so correct it to 51%, or "about half."

## 3. Internal inconsistencies

- **Number of sites:** Section 1 says **three** distribution sites. Section 3 says the van will serve **four**. Reconcile these. If the warehouse also distributes, say so.
- **Timetable is out of date:** Section 7 promises the equipment "in service by **October 2026**," which has already passed. Even ordering immediately on award, the cold room alone needs eight weeks, plus the time for the funder's decision. Give a realistic date, or a timetable relative to the award date.

## 4. Cost-per-meal claims are overstated

- The 33p figure (£48,600 ÷ 147,600 meals) is correct as a capital-only figure. But the application calls the project "sustainable," and the full first-year cost includes £11,000 of running costs. That makes it about **41p per meal**.
- The cover note says the cost falls "to almost nothing over the equipment's ten-year life." Over ten years, running costs (about £110,000, before any rise) would be more than double the capital cost. That gives roughly **11p per meal**, not "almost nothing." Still good value, but the claim as stated is easy to disprove.
- A ten-year life is reasonable for a cold room. It is not credible for a van that is already three years old with 40,000 miles and heavy daily use. Claim about five to seven years for the van, or budget for its replacement.
- The 147,600 meals assumes **all** 1.2 tonnes is accepted, stored, distributed and eaten every week. The application doesn't show that a 12 m³ cold room, the van's collection rounds, and three or four sites open on different days can handle that volume. Spoilage and stock rotation will reduce it. A cautious figure (for example, 80%) with a sensitivity note would be more convincing.

## 5. Evidence claimed in the cover note but missing from the document

The cover note says the declined food is precisely quantified because "we log every declined offer." The application only says "**around** 1.2 tonnes" and never mentions the log. That log is the strongest evidence you have, so put it in:
- describe the logging method;
- give the period covered;
- consider attaching a summary.

Likewise:
- "Clients, referrers and our own volunteers consistently tell us…" needs data, such as survey results or the number of referrer comments.
- The supermarkets' written confirmation should be attached or quoted. Note that "will continue to offer surplus" is not a volume commitment, and surplus levels can change.
- Competing quotes are mentioned but not attached. Funders usually require them.

## 6. Operational gaps an assessor will ask about

- **Who drives the van?** A loaded refrigerated van may exceed 3.5 tonnes, which would need a C1 licence. Volunteer drivers affect insurance costs and availability. Say who will drive and how often.
- **Food safety:** there is no mention of temperature monitoring, HACCP or food hygiene training, or Environmental Health registration for handling chilled and ready-meal stock.
- **Chilled storage at the sites:** the sites apparently have no refrigeration. Explain how chilled food is kept safe on distribution days.
- **Staffing:** two part-time staff will handle extra collections, stock rotation and handling of more than 60 tonnes a year. Show that volunteer capacity exists.
- **Budget:** state whether figures include VAT, and add a contingency (commonly 5–10% for installation and electrical work, which often overrun).

## 7. Monitoring

- Raising fresh-produce parcels from **under 10% to 80% within six months** is a big jump. Explain how it follows from the volumes, or set interim targets.
- The measures are mostly outputs (tonnes, proportion of parcels). The client survey has no target or defined question. Add at least one outcome measure, such as reported diet or satisfaction, and a measure of food wasted or spoiled after acceptance.

## 8. Tone

- "A modest capital investment" (Section 9) sits awkwardly next to a request equal to **half your annual income**. Stress value for money instead of modesty.
- "Permanently transforms" overstates things, given the running-cost and van-lifespan problems above.

## Summary

| Priority | Issue |
|---|---|
| Must fix | £11k/yr running costs with no funding source; sustainability section contradicts the finances |
| Must fix | 66% should be 51% |
| Must fix | Three vs four sites; October 2026 date already passed |
| Should fix | Cost-per-meal and ten-year van claims overstated; add running costs and realistic van life |
| Should fix | Put the decline log, supermarket letters and quotes in the application |
| Should fix | Drivers/licensing, food safety, site chilling, contingency, VAT |
| Improve | Realistic fresh-produce target; outcome measures; tone |

The underlying project is strong and well matched to a resilience fund. Its main weakness is that it presents itself as self-sustaining when its own figures show it isn't. If you address that openly with a credible running-cost plan, the application will be much more convincing than if an assessor finds the gap themselves.
